story: Gopa Iyer is first author of an Atlas study (IYE2012) that began with one bladder cancer patient who had a long remission on the mTOR inhibitor everolimus. Whole-genome sequencing of that tumor found a loss-of-function mutation in TSC1, a brake on mTOR. Checking 109 more bladder cancers, about 8 percent had TSC1 mutations, and these tracked with everolimus sensitivity. The starting point was a single patient, so it raises a hypothesis more than it proves one. PubMed lists Iyer at Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center.

highlights.IYE2012: First author: reported the genome sequencing of an exceptional everolimus responder and the link to TSC1 loss in bladder cancer.

studies.title: Genome sequencing identifies a basis for everolimus sensitivity
studies.finding: Genome sequencing of a single exceptional everolimus responder implicates TSC1 loss as the sensitivity basis. An n-of-1 observation, hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

story: Samson Hennessy-Strahs is first author of an Atlas study (HEN2026) on the immune cells that clear surfactant from the lungs, called alveolar macrophages. In mice, removing mTOR from myeloid cells, or treating the animals with the mTOR inhibitor temsirolimus, steadily wiped out these macrophages and caused a lung condition resembling pulmonary alveolar proteinosis. The work points to a possible cause of lung side effects seen with mTOR-inhibitor drugs. PubMed lists him at Texas A&M University and at Houston Methodist Hospital.

highlights.HEN2026: First author: reported that deleting or drugging mTOR in mice depletes alveolar macrophages and produces lung disease like that seen with mTOR-inhibitor drugs.

studies.finding: Myeloid-specific deletion of mTOR (and pharmacologic mTOR inhibition with temsirolimus) causes progressive depletion of alveolar macrophages, impaired phagocytosis, lipid accumulation and PAP-like lung pathology in mice, identifying mTOR as a nonredundant regulator of alveolar macrophage survival — mechanistic support for mTOR-inhibitor-associated pulmonary toxicity.

studies.finding: The paper that broke the simple 'metformin works through AMPK' story. Metformin still suppressed hepatic glucose production in mice and hepatocytes lacking AMPK or LKB1, acting instead through a fall in hepatic energy charge. story: Diogo Martins-Branco was first author of EVERGREEN, a 2026 multicentre study of women with ER-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer whose disease had progressed on a CDK4/6 inhibitor. Adding everolimus (an mTOR inhibitor) to hormone therapy gave a modest gain in progression-free survival, 5.0 versus 4.3 months, with no clear gain in overall survival. The study was retrospective and not randomised, so treatment-selection bias cannot be ruled out. PubMed lists Martins-Branco at the Institut Jules Bordet in Brussels.

story: BAS2012 (2012) is BOLERO-2, a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 women with hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer. Adding everolimus to exemestane roughly doubled progression-free survival (10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review). Mario Campone is a middle author in the author list. PIC2014 (2014) is the final overall-survival report of BOLERO-2. Median overall survival was 31.0 months with everolimus plus exemestane and 26.6 months with placebo plus exemestane, a difference that was not statistically significant. Mario Campone is a middle author in the author list.

PubMed gives no affiliation for this author in the BOLERO-2 primary report. The affiliation here comes from the final overall-survival report, which lists the same author by surname and initials and shares many co-authors with the primary report.

story: Joseph A Baur is last author of an Atlas study (LAM2012) on a puzzle about rapamycin. The drug extends lifespan in mice, yet long-term treatment makes them glucose intolerant and insulin resistant. The authors showed in mice that chronic rapamycin also disrupts a second complex, mTORC2, and that this loss explains the insulin problem. They also found that mice with less mTORC1 activity could live longer with normal glucose handling, so the two effects can be separated.

PubMed's record of this study lists no affiliation for Baur. The match to the University of Pennsylvania comes from a later paper by the same group (PMID 32268298), which shares four authors with this study and lists Joseph A Baur at the Institute for Diabetes, Obesity, and Metabolism there.

highlights.LAM2012: Last author: senior author of the mouse work showing that rapamycin disrupts mTORC2 and causes insulin resistance.

studies.title: Rapamycin-induced insulin resistance is mediated by mTORC2 loss and uncoupled from longevity

Rapamycin did break up mTORC2 (it separated mTOR from Rictor) in liver, fat and muscle, and deleting Rictor in the liver alone reproduced the glucose problem. story: Three studies in the Atlas list her as a co-author, in the middle of the author list each time. The first showed, in cells and mice, that mTORC1 phosphorylates the transcription factor TFEB through a special route that depends on RagC and RagD, and that this route drives kidney disease in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome.

The second, in cells, found that the stress-granule proteins G3BP1 and G3BP2 hold the TSC complex on the lysosome, which keeps mTORC1 in check. The third was a structural study that showed how mTORC1 reaches TFEB on two Rag-Ragulator complexes. PubMed lists her at the Institute of Cell Biology, Biocenter, Medical University of Innsbruck in all three.

studies.title: G3BPs tether the TSC complex to lysosomes and suppress mTORC1 signaling
studies.finding: Adds a physical brake upstream of mTORC1. G3BP1 and G3BP2, known until then as core stress-granule proteins, also sit on the cytoplasmic face of the lysosome and are what holds the TSC complex there; without them TSC cannot reach its target and mTORC1 becomes over-responsive to amino acids and insulin. Loss of G3BP1 reproduces TSC-like hyperactivity phenotypes: faster mTORC1-driven motility in breast cancer cells, with low G3BP1 correlating with worse patient outcome, and disturbed neuronal development in zebrafish. Relevant to the Atlas because it is a lysosomal tethering step that the canonical Rheb/TSC diagram does not show.

studies.title: Structure of the lysosomal mTORC1-TFEB-Rag-Ragulator megacomplex
studies.finding:
First structural view of how mTORC1 actually reaches TFEB to phosphorylate it: two full Rag-Ragulator complexes present a single TFEB molecule to the mTOR active site, one in the normal Raptor-docking arrangement and a second, non-canonical one that grips TFEB's own first helix. Mutating that grip point drives TFEB straight into the nucleus (turning on autophagy/lysosome genes) without disturbing where mTORC1 itself sits. Explains, at the level of atoms, why TFEB phosphorylation needs the tumour suppressor FLCN and the GDP-loaded state of RagC in a way the authors report for no other mTORC1 substrate.

studies.title: L-Arginine Modulates T Cell Metabolism and Enhances Survival and Anti-tumor Activity
studies.finding: Tracking metabolites and proteins in activated human T cells, the authors found intracellular L-arginine falls sharply after activation even in 1 mM medium, because uptake and conversion to ornithine, proline and spermidine rise. Raising L-arginine shifted metabolism from glycolysis towards oxidative phosphorylation, increased oxygen consumption and spare respiratory capacity, and produced central-memory-like cells (CCR7 and CD62L high, less IFN-gamma) with greater survival capacity; blocking arginase gave the same survival gain at physiological 150 uM L-arginine. studies.title: IDH3 regulates citrate homeostasis to control metabolic fitness and venetoclax resistance of AML stem cells
studies.finding: IDH3A loss in AML leukemic stem cells reduces TCA cycle flux and raises intracellular citrate, activating AMPK and suppressing mTORC1 (lowering translation), which sensitizes cells to BCL2 inhibition by venetoclax - nominating the IDH3A-citrate-AMPK-mTORC1 axis as a target to overcome venetoclax/azacitidine resistance.

current.lab_name: Institute of Translational Medicine, Zhejiang Shuren University (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
current.role: Senior (last) author of a 2026 mouse study on Lamtor5 loss, macrophage ageing and systemic ageing.
current.sub: Institute of Translational Medicine, Zhejiang Shuren University · Yuhang Institute of Medical Science Innovation and Transformation, Hangzhou, China
story: Liyun Shi was last author of a 2026 mouse study on immune ageing. The work showed that the mTOR-activating protein Lamtor5 declines with age and that its loss pushes macrophages into senescence and sets off cGAS-STING inflammation that spreads to other tissues. Restoring Lamtor5 in old mice eased these ageing signs. PubMed lists Shi at the Institute of Translational Medicine, Zhejiang Shuren University in Hangzhou.

highlights.LV2026: Last author of the study linking falling Lamtor5 to macrophage senescence and ageing in mice.

pubmed_affiliation: Key lab of Artificial Organs and Computational Medicine, Institute of Translational Medicine, Zhejiang Shuren University, Hangzhou, China.

studies.title: Age-associated decline of Lamtor5 drives immunosenescence and systemic aging via cGAS-mediated paracrine inflammation.
studies.finding: Age-driven loss of Lamtor5, a key lysosomal mTOR activation complex subunit, drives macrophage immunosenescence and systemic aging phenotypes in mice by unleashing cGAS-STING paracrine inflammation; restoring Lamtor5 in aged mice rescued immunosenescence and attenuated systemic ageing phenotypes.

current.lab_name: Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute (Ashburn, Virginia, USA)
current.role: First author of a 2018 crystal structure of arginine-bound SLC38A9, the lysosomal arginine transporter linked to mTORC1.
current.sub: Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute (PubMed affiliation, 2018)
story: Hsiang-Ting Lei was first author of a 2018 paper in Nature Structural and Molecular Biology (LEI2018), with three co-authors. The team solved the crystal structure of zebrafish SLC38A9 holding an arginine molecule. SLC38A9 sits on the lysosome and helps tell mTORC1 which amino acids are available, so the structure shows how that binding works.

highlights.LEI2018: First author of the SLC38A9 arginine crystal structure; PubMed lists the work at the Janelia Research Campus.

pubmed_affiliation: Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Ashburn, VA, USA.

studies.title: Crystal structure of arginine-bound lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 in the cytosol-open state
studies.finding: Crystal structure of arginine-bound SLC38A9 reveals the basis of lysosomal arginine sensing.

current.lab_name: Joslin Diabetes Center (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
current.role: First author of a 2012 study of TOR signalling, rapamycin and lifespan in worms through SKN-1 and DAF-16.
current.sub: Joslin Diabetes Center · Harvard Medical School, Boston, USA
story: In the worm C. elegans, blocking TORC1 genetically extended lifespan through SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO. Rapamycin also extended lifespan, but only through SKN-1 and not DAF-16, probably because it also affects TORC2. Rapamycin triggered a similar protective response in mice. Robida-Stubbs is the first of eight authors, and PubMed lists the Joslin Diabetes Center and Harvard Medical School.

highlights.ROB2012: First of eight authors on the worm study of TOR, rapamycin and lifespan through SKN-1 and DAF-16.

pubmed_affiliation: Joslin Diabetes Center, Harvard Stem Cell Institute, and Department of Genetics, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02215, USA.

studies.title: TOR signaling and rapamycin influence longevity by regulating SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO
studies.finding: In C. elegans, genetic TORC1 inhibition extends lifespan through SKN-1/Nrf and DAF-16/FoxO, whereas rapamycin's lifespan effect requires SKN-1 but not DAF-16, apparently because it also hits TORC2.

current.lab_name: Key Laboratory of Systems Health Science of Zhejiang Province, Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences (Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China)
current.role: First author of a review of nutrient-sensing pathways in adult stem cells.
current.sub: School of Life Science, Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
story: Tianxiong Xiao was first author of the Atlas study XIA2026 in Seminars in Cell & Developmental Biology. It is a review, not new experiments. It proposes that mTOR, AMPK, sirtuins and insulin/IGF-1 signalling work together to steer adult stem cells between rest, activation and differentiation. With age this network drifts out of balance, which may contribute to stem cell exhaustion. PubMed lists Xiao at the Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study.

highlights.XIA2026: First author: wrote the review on how nutrient-sensing pathways including mTOR control adult stem cells.

pubmed_affiliation: Key Laboratory of Systems Health Science of Zhejiang Province, School of Life Science, Hangzhou Institute for Advanced Study, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Hangzhou 310024, China.

studies.title: Nutrient-sensing pathways in adult stem cells: Orchestrating homeostasis, aging, and disease
studies.finding: Proposes an integrated framework in which mTOR, AMPK, sirtuins, and insulin/IGF-1 signaling jointly govern adult stem cell transitions between quiescence, activation, and differentiation; age-related dysregulation of this nutrient-sensing network drives stem cell exhaustion and tissue degeneration, and interventions (mTOR inhibitors, AMPK activators, NAD+ precursors, dietary strategies) can restore ASC function.

current.lab_name: Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
current.role: First author of a 2025 study on how mTOR briefly switches off APC/C to boost glycolysis at cell cycle entry.
current.sub: Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics · National Cancer Institute, Bethesda, USA
story: After a growth signal, mTOR quickly adds a phosphate to the APC/C helper protein CDH1, which partly releases it and briefly inactivates APC/C. The glycolysis enzyme PFKFB3 then builds up and glycolysis rises, until a later phosphatase restores APC/C. The pulse of glycolysis is needed for cells to enter the cell cycle. Paul is the first of thirteen authors, and PubMed lists the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda.

highlights.PAU2025: First of thirteen authors on the Nature paper on transient APC/C inactivation by mTOR.

pubmed_affiliation: Laboratory of Cancer Biology and Genetics, Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute, Bethesda, MD, USA.

studies.title: Transient APC/C inactivation by mTOR boosts glycolysis during cell cycle entry
studies.finding: After mitogen stimulation, mTOR quickly phosphorylates the APC/C adaptor CDH1, partly releasing it and briefly inactivating APC/C; the glycolytic enzyme PFKFB3 accumulates and glycolysis rises, until a delayed phosphatase restores APC/C. This incoherent feed-forward loop produces a pulse of glycolysis that cell cycle entry requires.

current.lab_name: Laboratory of Gene Regulation and Signal Transduction, Department of Pharmacology, School of Medicine, University of California San Diego (La Jolla, California, USA)
current.role: First author of a 2010 fruit fly study of Sestrin as a feedback inhibitor of TOR that guards against age-related damage.
current.sub: Department of Pharmacology, University of California San Diego School of Medicine (PubMed affiliation, 2010)
story: Jun Hee Lee was first author of a 2010 Science paper in the Atlas (LEE2010), listed at the University of California San Diego. In fruit flies, Sestrin rises when TOR stays active, and then pushes TOR back down. Flies without Sestrin built up fat and developed mitochondrial, muscle and heart problems that looked like ageing. Blocking TOR or switching on AMPK prevented these problems.

highlights.LEE2010: First author of the fruit fly study on Sestrin and TOR feedback.

pubmed_affiliation: Laboratory of Gene Regulation and Signal Transduction, Department of Pharmacology, School of Medicine, University of California San Diego (UCSD), La Jolla, CA 92093-0723, USA.

studies.title: Sestrin as a feedback inhibitor of TOR that prevents age-related pathologies
studies.finding: An early study linking Sestrin, later identified as a leucine sensor in mammals, to age-associated pathology in flies (fat accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, muscle and cardiac decline), prevented by TOR inhibition or AMPK activation. Sestrin sits in a negative feedback loop: TOR activity drives Sestrin expression, and Sestrin inhibits TOR back.
